# Page: Training System

# Training System

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/train.py](src/train.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

The Training System of SurPass orchestrates end-to-end model optimization, coordinating distributed data parallelism, multi-objective loss computation, specialized parameter grouping, learning rate scheduling, and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) weight tracking [src/train.py:1-36](). It binds dataset pipelines to the `ResOnly` architecture [src/train.py:35](), supervising both residue-level and inter-chain pairwise representations [src/train.py:168-182]().

This page provides a high-level overview of the training infrastructure. For detailed technical specifications, implementation routines, and mathematical formulations, refer to the child pages:
- [Training Loop and Distributed Execution](#4.1)
- [Loss Functions and Objectives](#4.2)
- [Optimizer, LR Schedules and EMA](#4.3)

---

## Architecture to Code Mapping

The following diagram illustrates how conceptual training operations map directly to codebase entities within `src/train.py`, `src/model/loss.py`, `src/model/optimizer.py`, and `src/model/ema.py`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Natural Language Space"
      A["Distributed Training Setup"] --> B["Epoch Execution & Logging"]
      B --> C["Multi-Objective Loss Computation"]
      C --> D["Optimizer & Parameter Grouping"]
      D --> E["Shadow Weight Maintenance"]
    end

    subgraph "Code Entity Space"
      A --> F["src/utils/ddp_utils.py:seed_everything"]
      A --> G["torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel"]
      B --> H["src/train.py:main"]
      C --> I["src/model/loss.py:FocalCELoss"]
      C --> J["src/model/loss.py:TverskyLoss"]
      D --> K["src/model/optimizer.py:get_optimizer"]
      D --> L["src/model/optimizer.py:get_lr_scheduler"]
      E --> M["src/model/ema.py:EMAWrapper"]
    end
```
*Sources: [src/train.py:1-36](), [src/model/loss.py:1-50](), [src/model/optimizer.py:1-50](), [src/model/ema.py:1-40]()*

---

## 4.1 Training Loop and Distributed Execution

The training entrypoint is anchored in `src/train.py`, managing distributed execution across multiple ranks using PyTorch DDP (`DistributedDataParallel`) [src/train.py:11](). It initializes environment seeds [src/train.py:36](), constructs distributed dataloaders with `DistributedWeightedSampler` [src/train.py:20](), executes training and evaluation epochs, handles gradient accumulation, and logs metrics (such as AUROC and AUPRC via scikit-learn [src/train.py:7-112]()) to Weights & Biases (`wandb`) [src/train.py:15-18]().

For detailed coverage of the training loop, DDP configuration, epoch cycles, checkpoint management, and metrics evaluation, see [Training Loop and Distributed Execution](#4.1).

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start["Hydra Config"] --> Init["src/train.py:main"]
    Init --> DDP["src/utils/ddp_utils.py:init_distributed"]
    DDP --> Load["src/data/collate.py:get_dataloader"]
    Load --> Loop["Epoch Training Loop"]
    Loop --> Forward["ResOnly Forward Pass"]
    Forward --> Loss["_compute_pair_losses"]
    Loss --> Backward["Backward & Step"]
    Backward --> Log["wandb Logging & Checkpoint"]
```
*Sources: [src/train.py:6-36](), [src/data/collate.py:21-25]() *

---

## 4.2 Loss Functions and Objectives

SurPass optimizes complex protein-protein interactions using a composite loss formulation defined in `src/model/loss.py`. The objective suite combines distogram supervision via Cross-Entropy, Focal loss, and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) [src/train.py:23-32](), along with Tversky loss [src/train.py:29]() to handle class imbalance in contact maps. Specialized binding losses (`ResidueBindLoss`, `ProteinBindLoss`) [src/train.py:27-28]() and consistency regularizers [src/train.py:24]() supervise inter-chain and intra-chain spatial relationships.

For a thorough breakdown of target generation, distance binning, masking strategies, and loss equations, see [Loss Functions and Objectives](#4.2).

```mermaid
graph LR
    Outputs["SurpassOutput"] --> Dist["Distogram CE/Focal/MAE"]
    Outputs --> Tversky["Tversky Loss"]
    Outputs --> ResBind["Residue Bind Loss"]
    Outputs --> ProtBind["Protein Bind Loss"]
    Outputs --> Consist["Consistency Loss"]
    Dist --> Total["Total Combined Loss"]
    Tversky --> Total
    ResBind --> Total
    ProtBind --> Total
    Consist --> Total
```
*Sources: [src/train.py:23-32](), [src/model/loss.py:1-100]()*

---

## 4.3 Optimizer, LR Schedules and EMA

Optimization and hyperparameter scheduling are modularized in `src/model/optimizer.py` and `src/model/ema.py`. The `get_optimizer` function constructs an `AdamW` optimizer with customized parameter grouping (e.g., separating weight decay for normalization layers or biases) [src/train.py:34](). Learning rate scheduling supports AlphaFold3-style warmups and cosine decay schedules via `get_lr_scheduler` [src/train.py:34](). Furthermore, `EMAWrapper` maintains shadow copies of model weights to stabilize evaluation and inference performance [src/train.py:33]().

For full details on parameter filtering, optimizer configuration, schedule curves, and EMA weight updating rules, see [Optimizer, LR Schedules and EMA](#4.3).

```mermaid
graph TD
    Params["Model Parameters"] --> Group["src/model/optimizer.py:get_optimizer"]
    Group --> Opt["AdamW Optimizer"]
    Opt --> Sched["src/model/optimizer.py:get_lr_scheduler"]
    Sched --> Update["Parameter Update"]
    Update --> EMA["src/model/ema.py:EMAWrapper"]
```
*Sources: [src/train.py:33-34](), [src/model/optimizer.py:1-60](), [src/model/ema.py:1-49]()*

# Page: Training Loop and Distributed Execution

# Training Loop and Distributed Execution

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/train.py](src/train.py)
- [src/utils/ddp_utils.py](src/utils/ddp_utils.py)

</details>



This page documents the training system entry point, distributed data parallel (DDP) initialization, epoch execution routines (`train_epoch` and `evaluate_epoch`), gradient accumulation, checkpoint management, Weights & Biases (`wandb`) integration, and performance metric computation.

---

## 1. Initialization and Distributed Execution Setup

The training pipeline is initiated via the Hydra-configured entry point function `main()` in `src/train.py`. The setup process configures deterministic random seeding, detects and initializes distributed training environments, wraps models with PyTorch's `DistributedDataParallel` (DDP), and instantiates optimizers, learning rate schedulers, and exponential moving average (EMA) wrappers.

Distributed execution metadata is managed by the `DistWrapper` class [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:12-34](), which inspects environment variables like `RANK`, `LOCAL_RANK`, `WORLD_SIZE`, and `LOCAL_WORLD_SIZE`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Hydra Config (cfg)"] --> B["seed_everything()"]
    B --> C["DistWrapper (src/utils/ddp_utils.py)"]
    C --> D["torch.distributed.init_process_group"]
    D --> E["ResOnly Model Initialization"]
    E --> F["DistributedDataParallel (DDP)"]
    F --> G["get_optimizer() & get_lr_scheduler()"]
    G --> H["EMAWrapper Initialization"]
```
*Sources: [src/train.py:1-50](), [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:1-49]()*

The function `seed_everything(seed, deterministic)` sets random seeds across `random`, `numpy`, and `torch`, and configures CuDNN determinism when requested [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:37-49](). Log messages are filtered by rank via `log_info(message)` to ensure only rank 0 writes to standard output [src/train.py:47-50]().

---

## 2. Epoch Execution: Training and Evaluation Loops

Data loading leverages distributed sampling (`DistributedWeightedSampler`) combined with `get_dataloader` [src/train.py:20-21](). Tensors are moved to the target hardware accelerator device using `to_device(obj, device)` [src/train.py:60-74](), supporting nested dictionaries and individual tensors.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["DataLoader Batches"] --> B["to_device(batch, device)"]
    B --> C["Forward Pass: ResOnly"]
    C --> D["SurpassOutput"]
    D --> E["_compute_pair_losses()"]
    E --> F["Backward Pass & Gradient Accumulation"]
    F --> G["Optimizer Step & LR Scheduler"]
    G --> H["EMAWrapper Update"]
```
*Sources: [src/train.py:60-193]()*

During the training epoch:
1. Batches are fetched from the distributed data loader.
2. Inputs are transferred to the accelerator device using `to_device` [src/train.py:60-74]().
3. The forward pass computes residue and pair representations through the `ResOnly` model, returning a `SurpassOutput` container [src/train.py:35]().
4. Losses are computed via helper routines like `_compute_pair_losses` [src/train.py:168-193](), which evaluates specific loss terms (such as distogram cross-entropy, focal loss, Tversky loss, and binding objectives).
5. Gradient accumulation and optimizer stepping update model weights, followed by EMA shadow weight updates via `EMAWrapper` [src/train.py:33]().

---

## 3. Metrics, Logging, and Checkpointing

Evaluation routines assess model performance on validation sets without updating model weights. Key validation tasks include binary classification metrics calculation and residue/protein-level contact scoring.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Model Logits / Output"] --> B["pair_bind_scores()"]
    B --> C["_binary_classification_metrics()"]
    C --> D["AUROC & AUPRC Calculation"]
    D --> E["Wandb Logging"]
    E --> F["Checkpoint Saving"]
```
*Sources: [src/train.py:77-113](), [src/train.py:140-165]()`

### Key Evaluation Functions
* `_binary_classification_metrics(scores, target, positive_weight)`: Computes Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under Curve (AUROC) and Precision-Recall Area Under Curve (AUPRC) using scikit-learn (`roc_curve`, `auc`, `average_precision_score`), supporting optional positive class weighting [src/train.py:92-113]().
* `pair_bind_scores(logits, pair_mask, p1_length, contact_bins, ppi_score_threshold, p2_length)`: Converts distogram logits into contact probabilities via softmax, applies inter-chain masks via `inter_chain_pair_mask` [src/train.py:22](), and extracts maximum binding probabilities (`p_bind`) and contact counts (`n_contacts`) [src/train.py:140-165]().
* `_region_masks(pair_mask, label_mask, p1_length, p2_length)`: Separates contact and pair maps into intra-chain and inter-chain regions to isolate protein-protein interaction (PPI) supervision signals [src/train.py:115-137]().

Logging is integrated with `wandb` (Weights & Biases) when available [src/train.py:15-18](), tracking training loss components, learning rates, and validation metrics across distributed ranks. Checkpoints capture model weights, optimizer states, scheduler states, and EMA parameters.

*Sources: [src/train.py:1-193](), [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:1-49]()*

---

# Page: Loss Functions and Objectives

# Loss Functions and Objectives

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [configs/train.yaml](configs/train.yaml)
- [src/model/loss.py](src/model/loss.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page documents the loss functions, target generation schemes, masking strategies, and supervision objectives implemented in SurPass for training protein-protein interaction (PPI) and inter-chain contact prediction models. The loss architecture balances local intra-chain geometry with global inter-chain contacts using a combination of distogram cross-entropy, focal cross-entropy, mean absolute error (MAE) on expected distances, Tversky similarity for contact maps, residue-level and protein-level binding heads, and consistency regularizers.

Sources: [`configs/train.yaml:69-91](), [`src/model/loss.py:1-197]()

---

## Loss Configuration & Hyperparameters

The loss configuration is defined in `configs/train.yaml` under the `loss` block. These hyperparameters dictate the relative weighting of intra-chain versus inter-chain components, focal modulation parameters, and specialized binding objectives.

```yaml
loss:
  intra: 0.3
  inter: 0.7
  inter_neg_per_pos: 10.0
  focal:
    weight: 1.0
    gamma: 1.5
    alpha: 5.0
  mae:
    weight: 0.2
  tversky:
    weight: 1.0
    alpha: 0.7
    beta: 0.3
  residue_bind:
    weight: 1.0
    neg_per_pos: 0.0
    negative_pair_weight: 0.25
  protein:
    weight: 1.0
  consistency:
    weight: 0.1
```

Sources: [`configs/train.yaml:69-91]()

---

## Target Generation and Distance Binning

Pairwise distances are discretized into bins to formulate classification and regression targets. The function `distance_bin_centers()` computes the center of each distance bin given linear spacing limits.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Distance Limits (bin_start, bin_end, bin_count)"] --> B["distance_bin_centers()"]
    B --> C["Linear Bin Edges (torch.linspace)"]
    C --> D["First & Last Bin Width Extrapolation"]
    D --> E["Bin Center Tensors (torch.Tensor)"]

    style A fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style B fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style C fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style D fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style E fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```
*Figure 1: Natural Language to Code Entity Space mapping for distance binning.*

The distance bin centers and supervision flags are initialized in `src/model/loss.py`:
- `distance_bin_centers()` [src/model/loss.py:6-26]: Constructs bin centers for regression and evaluation.
- `distogram_supervision()` [src/model/loss.py:78-92]: Derives contact indicators (`is_contact`), softmax probabilities (`pair_probs`), and contact probabilities (`contact_probability`) from raw network logits.

Sources: [`src/model/loss.py:6-92]()

---

## Distance and Contact Loss Modules

SurPass employs several loss modules operating on pairwise logits and target bins, partitioned by intra-chain and inter-chain masks.

### 1. Distogram Cross-Entropy (`DistogramCELoss`)
Calculates masked cross-entropy over pairwise distance bins across the predicted logit tensor and target bins [src/model/loss.py:113-129].

```python
class DistogramCELoss(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, logits, target_bins, mask):
        loss = F.cross_entropy(
            logits.permute(0, 3, 1, 2),
            target_bins.long(),
            reduction="none",
        )
        return _masked_mean(loss, mask)
```

### 2. Focal Cross-Entropy (`FocalCELoss`)
Applies modulating factors to address class imbalance between contact and non-contact pairs, scaling losses by a contact-bin `alpha` factor and modulating by `(1 - p_t)^gamma` [src/model/loss.py:131-172]. It returns separate intra-chain and inter-chain losses.

### 3. Distogram Mean Absolute Error (`DistogramMAELoss`)
Computes the L1 error between the expected distance (calculated via softmax probabilities over `bin_centers`) and the target bin center, masked appropriately [src/model/loss.py:174-197].

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Raw Model Logits (logits)"] --> B["distogram_supervision()"]
    B --> C["DistogramCELoss"]
    B --> D["FocalCELoss"]
    B --> E["DistogramMAELoss"]
    C --> F["Combined Loss Total"]
    D --> F
    E --> F

    style A fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style B fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style C fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style D fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style E fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style F fill:#fff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```
*Figure 2: Loss computation data flow through supervision and individual loss modules.*

Sources: [`src/model/loss.py:113-197]()

---

## Masking and Partitioning

Loss calculations are strictly governed by masks to isolate intra-chain contacts from inter-chain interactions:
- **Intra-chain Mask (`intra_mask`)**: Restricts loss evaluation to residue pairs belonging to the same protein chain.
- **Inter-chain Mask (`inter_mask`)**: Restricts loss evaluation to residue pairs spanning different interacting chains.
- **Masked Mean (`_masked_mean`)**: Normalizes loss sums by the count of valid unmasked elements, clamping the denominator to a minimum of `1.0` to avoid division by zero [src/model/loss.py:29-32].

Sources: [`src/model/loss.py:29-32](), [`src/model/loss.py:131-197]()

---

# Page: Optimizer, LR Schedules and EMA

# Optimizer, LR Schedules and EMA

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/model/components/triangle_update.py](src/model/components/triangle_update.py)
- [src/model/ema.py](src/model/ema.py)
- [src/model/optimizer.py](src/model/optimizer.py)
- [src/utils/model_utils.py](src/utils/model_utils.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page documents the training optimization infrastructure in SurPass, located in `src/model/optimizer.py` and `src/model/ema.py`. It covers parameter grouping strategies for weight decay in `get_adamw`, standard and fused optimizer initialization (`get_optimizer`), learning rate schedules (`AlphaFold3LRScheduler` and `CosineAnnealingWithWarmup`), and shadow weight management via `EMAWrapper`.

---

## 1. Optimizer Configuration and Parameter Grouping

The optimization setup distinguishes between weights that benefit from L2 regularization (weight decay) and those that do not (biases and layer normalization parameters). 

### Parameter Grouping in `get_adamw`
The function `get_adamw()` inspects model parameters that require gradients (`[src/model/optimizer.py:30-33]()`). It separates them into two distinct groups based on tensor dimensionality (`[src/model/optimizer.py:34-41]()`):
- **Decay Parameters**: Tensors with dimensionality $\ge 2$ (such as weight matrices in matrix multiplications and embedding layers) receive the specified `weight_decay`.
- **Non-Decay Parameters**: Tensors with dimensionality $< 2$ (such as biases and LayerNorm parameters) have their `weight_decay` set explicitly to `0.0`.

Additionally, `get_adamw()` checks for CUDA availability and fused optimizer support in `torch.optim.AdamW`, enabling fused execution (`fused=True`) when possible (`[src/model/optimizer.py:50-57]()`).

```mermaid
graph TD
    Model["torch.nn.Module"] -->|named_parameters| Filter["Filter requires_grad=True"]
    Filter -->|dim >= 2| Decay["decay_params (Weights & Embeddings)"]
    Filter -->|dim < 2| NoDecay["nodecay_params (Biases & LayerNorm)"]
    Decay -->|weight_decay=wd| Group["optim_groups"]
    NoDecay -->|weight_decay=0.0| Group
    Group -->|Check Fused| AdamW["torch.optim.AdamW src/model/optimizer.py:54-56"]
```
*Sources: [src/model/optimizer.py:10-59]()*, *[src/model/optimizer.py:62-84]()*

---

## 2. Learning Rate Schedulers

SurPass provides a factory function `get_lr_scheduler()` (`[src/model/optimizer.py:170-192]()`) that instantiates learning rate schedulers compatible with PyTorch's `LRScheduler` interface.

### AlphaFold3 Learning Rate Scheduler
`AlphaFold3LRScheduler` implements the training schedule described in AlphaFold 3 (`[src/model/optimizer.py:132-141]()`). It features:
- A linear warmup phase during the initial `warmup_steps` (`[src/model/optimizer.py:151-152]()`).
- Periodic step-wise decays every `decay_every_n_steps`, scaling the learning rate by `decay_factor` (`[src/model/optimizer.py:154-155]()`).

### Cosine Annealing with Warmup
`CosineAnnealingWithWarmup` provides a smooth decay profile (`[src/model/optimizer.py:87-114]()`):
- Linear warmup up to `warmup_steps` (`[src/model/optimizer.py:104-105]()`).
- Cosine decay curve down to `min_lr` across `decay_steps` (`[src/model/optimizer.py:109-114]()`).

```mermaid
graph TD
    SchedulerFactory["get_lr_scheduler() src/model/optimizer.py:170-192"] -->|lr_scheduler='af3'| AF3["AlphaFold3LRScheduler src/model/optimizer.py:132-169"]
    SchedulerFactory -->|lr_scheduler='cosine_annealing'| Cosine["CosineAnnealingWithWarmup src/model/optimizer.py:87-130"]
    AF3 -->|Step Check| AF3Calc["Linear Warmup or Step Decay Formula"]
    Cosine -->|Step Check| CosineCalc["Linear Warmup or Cosine Curve Formula"]
```
*Sources: [src/model/optimizer.py:87-192]()*

---

## 3. Exponential Moving Average (EMA) Wrapper

To stabilize model evaluation and improve generalization, `EMAWrapper` (`[src/model/ema.py:4-50]`) maintains an exponential moving average of model weights.

### Lifecycle and Operations
1. **Registration**: `register()` clones the initial parameters of the model into a `self.shadow` dictionary (`[src/model/ema.py:23-26]()`).
2. **Update**: `update()` computes the exponential average at each step:
   $$\theta_{\text{shadow}} = (1 - \text{decay}) \cdot \theta_{\text{param}} + \text{decay} \cdot \theta_{\text{shadow}}$$
   Parameters can be selectively filtered using `mutable_param_keywords` (`[src/model/ema.py:27-38]()`).
3. **Shadow Application**: `apply_shadow()` backs up current model weights to `self.backup` and swaps them with `self.shadow` weights for evaluation (`[src/model/ema.py:39-44]()`).
4. **Restoration**: `restore()` puts the backed-up training weights back into the model (`[src/model/ema.py:45-49]()`).

```mermaid
graph TD
    Init["EMAWrapper.__init__() src/model/ema.py:4-14"] -->|register()| Reg["Clone weights to self.shadow src/model/ema.py:23-26"]
    Reg -->|Training Step| Upd["EMAWrapper.update() src/model/ema.py:27-38"]
    Upd -->|Evaluate Model| Apply["EMAWrapper.apply_shadow() src/model/ema.py:39-44"]
    Apply -->|Resume Training| Rest["EMAWrapper.restore() src/model/ema.py:45-50"]
```
*Sources: [src/model/ema.py:4-49]()*

---

## Purpose and Scope

Section 5 covers the execution of trained SurPass models on new or benchmark protein pairs, producing protein-, residue-, and pair-level interaction predictions. This workflow handles raw input data ingestion from FASTA files and precomputed protein language model (pLM) embeddings, supports long-sequence tiling via windowing strategies, and provides diagnostic utilities for monitoring tensors and visualizing distance maps.

As a parent page, this section provides a high-level overview of the inference ecosystem. For in-depth technical details, refer to the following child pages:
- [Inference Pipeline](#5.1) — Details on `InferencePairDataset`, dataset loading, prediction heads, and evaluation outputs (`[src/inference.py:157-192]()`).
- [Long-Sequence Windowing](#5.2) — Details on `src/utils/ppi_windows.py` and sequence tiling (`[src/utils/ppi_windows.py:1-50]()`).
- [Preview and Debugging Utilities](#5.3) — Details on `src/preview.py` for distance map visualization and debugging (`[src/preview.py:1-50]()`).

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Input Data: FASTA & Embeddings"] --> B["Dataset Loading: InferencePairDataset"]
    B --> C["Model Execution: ResOnly"]
    C --> D["Prediction Heads: protein, residue, pair"]
    D --> E["Evaluation & Metrics: TSV/CSV/.pt outputs"]

    sub5_1["Inference Pipeline"] --> A
    sub5_1 --> B
    sub5_1 --> C
    sub5_1 --> D
    sub5_1 --> E
```
*Figure 5.1: High-level overview of the inference and evaluation pipeline bridging input data files to model prediction outputs.*

Sources: `[src/inference.py:1-192]()`

---

## 5.1. Inference Pipeline

The inference pipeline ingests test set manifests (TSVs) specifying protein pairs, matches them with FASTA sequence records, and loads precomputed pLM embeddings from disk `[src/inference.py:157-192]()`. The `InferencePairDataset` class structures these components into paired inputs suitable for batching via `inference_collate_fn` and `collate_concatenated_pairs` `[src/inference.py:151-192]()`.

Model predictions are evaluated across multiple interaction heads (`protein`, `residue`, and `pair`) defined in `PPI_HEADS` `[src/inference.py:33-46]`. Binary classification metrics and scores are logged and exported to structured formats such as TSV, CSV, or PyTorch tensors.

For comprehensive details on data loading, prediction heads, and evaluation metrics, see [Inference Pipeline](#5.1).

Sources: `[src/inference.py:33-192]()`

---

## 5.2. Long-Sequence Windowing

Protein complexes that exceed standard memory or sequence length limits cannot be processed in a single pass without severe GPU memory constraints. To resolve this, SurPass implements a windowing utility module in `src/utils/ppi_windows.py`.

The function `plan_ppi_windows` computes sliding-window partitions across long chain pairs, enabling localized feature extraction and model inference. The resulting sub-window predictions are subsequently aggregated back to the full sequence length using max-pooled strategies.

For detailed algorithms on tiling schedules, overlapping window management, and aggregation logic, see [Long-Sequence Windowing](#5.2).

Sources: `[src/utils/ppi_windows.py:1-60]()`

---

## 5.3. Preview and Debugging Utilities

SurPass provides dedicated diagnostic utilities in `src/preview.py` to inspect intermediate model states during inference and training. These utilities include distance map generation and visualization helpers, automated NaN and anomaly monitoring for model activations, and tensor utility functions.

These tools allow developers to debug spatial predictions, inspect distogram outputs, and verify tensor shape transformations across network layers.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Model Tensors & Distograms"] --> B["src/preview.py"]
    B --> C["Distance Map Visualization"]
    B --> D["NaN & Activation Monitoring"]
    B --> E["Tensor Inspection Utilities"]

    sub5_3["Preview and Debugging Utilities"] --> B
    sub5_3 --> C
    sub5_3 --> D
    sub5_3 --> E
```
*Figure 5.2: Diagnostic tooling architecture centering around `src/preview.py` for visualization and tensor inspection.*

For code-level documentation on visualization functions and tensor monitoring routines, see [Preview and Debugging Utilities](#5.3).

Sources: `[src/preview.py:1-50]()`

---

# Page: Inference Pipeline

# Inference Pipeline

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [configs/inference.yaml](configs/inference.yaml)
- [src/inference.py](src/inference.py)

</details>



The inference pipeline executes trained `ResOnly` models on protein-protein interaction (PPI) test sets [src/inference.py:17](). It ingests structural protein sequences from FASTA files [src/inference.py:78](), pre-computed protein Language Model (pLM) embeddings [src/inference.py:114](), and test metadata TSVs [src/inference.py:167](). It coordinates data batching [src/inference.py:151](), long-sequence windowing via `plan_ppi_windows` [src/inference.py:30](), multi-head prediction scoring across protein, residue, and pair levels [src/inference.py:33](), and output generation.

Sources: [src/inference.py:1-47](), [src/inference.py:78-155](), [src/inference.py:157-192]()

---

## Configuration System (`configs/inference.yaml`)

The inference configuration governs model architecture hyperparameters, input data directories, threshold settings, and execution flags. It maps directly to model construction and dataset instantiation routines.

| Configuration Block | Key Parameters | Code Mapping |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `data` | `test_set_tsv`, `fasta_path`, `embedding_dir`, `max_full_length`, `contact_threshold` | `InferencePairDataset` [src/inference.py:157-192]() |
| `model` | `n_layers`, `dim_token`, `dim_pair`, `n_heads`, `plm_in_dim`, `plm_out_dim` | `ResOnly` [src/inference.py:17]() |
| `metrics` | `positive_weight` | Evaluation weighting [src/inference.py:22-24]() |
| `performance` | `checkpoint_pair_blocks` | Gradient checkpointing flags [src/inference.py:46-48]() |

```yaml
# configs/inference.yaml excerpt
task_prefix: infer
seed: 42
ckpt_dir: null
data:
  test_set_tsv: ${data.root_dir}/test_set.tsv
  fasta_path: ${data.root_dir}/test_set.fasta
  embedding_dir: ${data.root_dir}/embeddings
model:
  n_layers: 8
  dim_token: 768
  dim_pair: 512
```

Sources: [configs/inference.yaml:1-52]()

---

### FASTA and Embedding Parsers
- **`load_fasta_sequences`**: Reads FASTA files sequentially, validates identifiers and non-empty sequences, and outputs a dictionary mapping protein IDs to uppercase sequence strings [src/inference.py:78-111]().
- **`load_plm_embedding`**: Loads pre-computed embedding files supporting raw `torch.Tensor` objects or nested dictionary wrappers containing the `plm_emb` key, coercing types to `torch.float32` [src/inference.py:114-120]().
- **`encode_residue_types`**: Maps residue characters to integer vocabularies using `restype_order` with fallback to `unk_restype_index` [src/inference.py:12-14](), [src/inference.py:123-127]().
- **`build_residue_features`**: Combines token embeddings, residue codes, positions, and masks into a standard feature dictionary [src/inference.py:130-148]().

Sources: [src/inference.py:78-148]()

### Dataset and Collation
`InferencePairDataset` iterates through the test set TSV metadata, resolves protein pairs via `parse_protein_pair`, checks sequence presence, and caches valid query items [src/inference.py:157-192](). The helper `inference_collate_fn` unpacks batch tuples and delegates pairing concatenation to `collate_concatenated_pairs` [src/inference.py:151-155]().

Sources: [src/inference.py:151-192]()

# Page: Long-Sequence Windowing

# Long-Sequence Windowing

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/inference.py](src/inference.py)
- [src/utils/ppi_windows.py](src/utils/ppi_windows.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

Protein complexes that exceed the maximum inference length budget (`budget`) cannot be processed in a single forward pass without running out of memory or violating model dimension constraints. The module `src/utils/ppi_windows.py` implements a sequence tiling strategy (`plan_ppi_windows`) that divides long protein complexes into smaller, non-overlapping contiguous spatial windows (`contiguous_spans`) while minimizing the total number of model evaluations (forward passes). 

This page details the mathematical and algorithmic design of window planning, chunk generation, and optimization heuristics used during long-sequence inference.

Sources: [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:1-7]()

---

## Window Planning and Tiling Architecture (`src/utils/ppi_windows.py`)

When a protein complex consisting of two chains with lengths `length_1` and `length_2` exceeds the allowed `budget` (defined as the maximum concatenated length of one forward pass), the system must partition the chains. Cutting both chains indiscriminately multiplies the number of required model evaluations (`k1 * k2`). The planner therefore searches for optimal window counts (`count_1`, `count_2`) that satisfy the budget constraint while preferring single-chain splitting over dual-chain splitting.

### Helper Functions: Ceiling Division and Spans

The module relies on basic partitioning primitives:
- `_ceil_div(numerator, denominator)`: Computes the ceiling division integer `(numerator + denominator - 1) // denominator` [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:12-14]().
- `contiguous_spans(length, count)`: Splits an interval `[0, length)` into `count` non-overlapping contiguous spans where span lengths differ by at most one, placing longer spans first [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:16-38]().

```python
# Conceptual view of span generation
def contiguous_spans(length: int, count: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    ...
```

Sources: [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:12-38]()

### Optimization Strategy: `choose_window_counts`

The core optimization routine `choose_window_counts(length_1, length_2, budget)` iterates over possible window partition counts to find the minimum number of rounds (`k1 * k2`) [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:41-86](). 

Feasibility is determined by the condition:
$$\lceil \text{length\_1} / k_1 \rceil + \lceil \text{length\_2} / k_2 \rceil \le \text{budget}$$

Tie-breaking rules prioritize:
1. Minimizing total forward rounds (`rounds = count_1 * count_2`).
2. Minimizing the rank of single-chain splits (`min(count_1, count_2)`), preferring to cut only one chain rather than both.
3. Cutting the longer chain when applicable [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:71-78]().

Sources: [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:41-86]()

### Window Generation: `plan_ppi_windows`

The public entrypoint `plan_ppi_windows(length_1, length_2, budget)` integrates span creation and window counts [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:89-121](). If `budget` is `None` or the sum of lengths is within the budget, a single window covering both chains `((0, length_1), (0, length_2))` is returned [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:107-108](). Otherwise, it invokes `choose_window_counts` and generates a list of paired intervals `((start_1, end_1), (start_2, end_2))` [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:111-114]().

Sources: [src/utils/ppi_windows.py:89-121]()

---

# Preview and Debugging Utilities

<details>

</details>



## Purpose and Scope
Section 5.3 covers the diagnostic and visualization utilities implemented in `src/preview.py` and `src/utils/nan_monitor.py`. These tools provide insight into model predictions by converting categorical distogram bins into continuous physical distance maps, rendering side-by-side comparison figures with chain boundaries, and monitoring training stability through deep tensor scanning, forward hook probing, and automated non-finite (NaN/Inf) root-cause classification.

Sources: `[src/preview.py:1-196]()`, `[src/utils/nan_monitor.py:1-217]()`

---

## Distance Map Visualization and Binned Utilities (`src/preview.py`)

The preview module (`src/preview.py`) loads checkpoints, runs inference on a subset of validation or training examples, and saves visual representations of true distance labels versus predicted distance maps.

### Key Functions
- **`distance_bin_centers(bin_start: float, bin_end: float, bin_count: int) -> torch.Tensor`**: Computes the physical distance boundaries and center points corresponding to discrete distogram classification bins `[src/preview.py:28-48]()`.
- **`bins_to_distance(bins: torch.Tensor, centers: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor`**: Maps discrete bin index predictions back to continuous physical distance values using precomputed `centers` `[src/preview.py:51-53]()`.
- **`masked_distance_map(bins: torch.Tensor, centers: torch.Tensor, valid_mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor`**: Applies `valid_mask` to distance matrices, setting invalid or masked pairs to `NaN` for visualization purposes `[src/preview.py:55-62]()`.
- **`save_distance_pair_figure(label_map, pred_map, output_path, p1_length)`**: Generates a side-by-side matplotlib figure comparing ground truth and prediction matrices using a `viridis` colormap where invalid/NaN entries are rendered in light gray. It invokes `_draw_chain_margin` to delineate multi-chain interfaces `[src/preview.py:64-110]()`.
- **`summarize_prediction(pred_bins, valid_mask, last_bin) -> str`**: Computes diagnostic string metrics including valid pair counts, unique predicted bins, and the fraction of pairs falling into the furthest distance bin (`far_bin_frac`) `[src/preview.py:112-126]()`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["DataLoader"] -->|Batch| B["ResOnly Model"]
    B -->|Logits / Bins| C["bins_to_distance"]
    C -->|Continuous Distances| D["masked_distance_map"]
    D -->|Valid Masked Array| E["save_distance_pair_figure"]
    E -->|PNG Figure| F["preview/ Output Directory"]

    classDef default fill:#fff,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px;
    linkStyle default stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px;
```
*Figure 1: Data flow in `src/preview.py` from raw model output to saved distance map figures.*

Sources: `[src/preview.py:28-126]()`

---

## NaN Monitoring and Numerical Diagnostics (`src/utils/nan_monitor.py`)

To prevent training instability or gradient poisoning from propagating through `AdamW`, `src/utils/nan_monitor.py` provides tensor inspection utilities, forward hook probing, and root-cause classification.

### Key Components & Functions
- **`NonFiniteTrainingError`**: A custom `RuntimeError` raised immediately upon detecting non-finite losses or gradients `[src/utils/nan_monitor.py:28-30]()`.
- **`finite_stats(name: str, value: Any) -> dict[str, Any]`**: Recursively traverses nested pytrees of tensors (`_as_tensors`), calculating total element counts, counts of `NaN` and `Inf` entries, and the absolute maximum value (`abs_max`) across floating-point elements `[src/utils/nan_monitor.py:32-80]()`.
- **`probe_first_nonfinite_module(model: nn.Module, residue_batch: dict) -> list[dict]`**: Attaches temporary forward hooks to watched submodules (`residue_embedder`, `outer_product_mean`, `pair_blocks`, etc.) to isolate the exact layer producing non-finite outputs from finite inputs (`true_risk`) `[src/utils/nan_monitor.py:122-166]()`.
- **`classify_nan_cause(report: dict[str, Any]) -> str`**: Analyzes a diagnostic report dictionary to categorize failure modes into clean categories: `dirty_input`, `empty_residue_mask`, `forward` layer overflows, `loss` term explosions, or `backward` gradient anomalies `[src/utils/nan_monitor.py:169-217]()`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Model Forward Pass"] -->|Inputs/Outputs| B["finite_stats"]
    B -->|Check NaN/Inf| C{"Is Finite?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Continue Training"]
    C -->|No| E["probe_first_nonfinite_module"]
    E -->|Trigger Hooks| F["classify_nan_cause"]
    F -->|Raise Error| G["NonFiniteTrainingError"]

    classDef default fill:#fff,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px;
    linkStyle default stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px;
```
*Figure 2: Execution flow of numerical debugging and exception handling in `src/utils/nan_monitor.py`.*

Sources: `[src/utils/nan_monitor.py:32-217]()`

## 6.1 Residue and Atom Constants

The `src/common` package houses domain-specific constants that define how amino acids, backbone atoms, and sidechains are encoded within tensors. These definitions establish standard amino acid indexing, one-letter/three-letter conversions, and the `atom14` atomic representation scheme commonly adopted in structural biology pipelines.

# Page: Residue and Atom Constants

# Residue and Atom Constants

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/common/atom_constants.py](src/common/atom_constants.py)
- [src/common/residue_constants.py](src/common/residue_constants.py)

</details>



### Purpose and Scope
This page documents the foundational chemical, atomic, and residue-level constants defined in `src/common/residue_constants.py` and `src/common/atom_constants.py`. These modules establish the fundamental vocabulary, amino acid dictionaries, atom type universes, the AlphaFold-style `atom14` coordinate padding representation, and chemical/hydrogen-bonding parameters adapted from MaSIF. They are consumed across data loading, geometric cropping, structural feature extraction, and evaluation pipelines within SurPass.

---

## 1. Residue Vocabularies and Mappings

The codebase defines standard representations for the 20 canonical amino acids, alongside handling for unknown or padding residues (`'X'` / `'UNK'`). These mappings provide bidirectional lookups between single-letter codes, three-letter codes, and integer indices.

* **Standard Residues (`restypes`)**: An alphabetically sorted list of the 20 standard single-letter amino acid codes [src/common/residue_constants.py:43-46]().
* **Integer Encodings**: `restype_order` maps single-letter codes to contiguous integers `0` through `19` [src/common/residue_constants.py:47](). An extended vocabulary `restypes_with_x` appends `'X'` for unknown residues at index `20` (`unk_restype_index`) [src/common/residue_constants.py:49-51]().
* **Code Converters**: Dictionaries `restype_1to3` and `restype_3to1` facilitate conversion between single-letter codes and three-letter residue names (e.g., `'A'` to `'ALA'`, `'X'` to `'UNK'`) [src/common/residue_constants.py:54-77]().

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["SingleLetterAA ('A', 'R', 'N'...)"] --> B["restypes (src/common/residue_constants.py:43-46)"]
    B --> C["restype_order (src/common/residue_constants.py:47)"]
    A --> D["restype_1to3 (src/common/residue_constants.py:54-76)"]
    D --> E["ThreeLetterAA ('ALA', 'ARG'...)"]
    E --> F["restype_3to1 (src/common/residue_constants.py:77)"]
    G["UnknownAA ('X')"] --> H["restypes_with_x (src/common/residue_constants.py:51)"]
```
*Sources: [src/common/residue_constants.py:43-77]()*

---

## 2. Atom Types and the `atom14` Representation

To handle variable numbers of side-chain atoms across different amino acid types while maintaining fixed-size tensor shapes (common in AlphaFold-derived architectures), SurPass utilizes a universal atom registry and a compact 14-atom per residue layout (`atom14`).

* **Universal Atom Universe (`atom_types`)**: A complete list of 37 unique heavy and polar hydrogen atom names encountered across standard amino acids, ranging from backbone atoms (`'N'`, `'CA'`, `'C'`, `'O'`, `'OXT'`) to specialized side-chain atoms (`'CG1'`, `'OG'`, `'SD'`, `'CZ2'`, etc.) [src/common/residue_constants.py:1-6]().
* **Atom Ordering**: `atom_order` maps each atom name string to its integer index in `atom_types` [src/common/residue_constants.py:7]().
* **`atom14` Encoding (`restype_name_to_atom14_names`)**: A dictionary mapping 3-letter residue names to a fixed-length list of 14 atom names [src/common/residue_constants.py:13-36](). Amino acids with fewer than 14 atoms (such as Glycine or Alanine) have their remaining slots padded with empty strings `''`.

```mermaid
graph TD
    AA["ThreeLetterName ('ALA', 'ARG', 'GLY'...)"] --> Dict["restype_name_to_atom14_names (src/common/residue_constants.py:13-36)"]
    Dict --> Array["Fixed 14-Element Atom List"]
    Array --> Pad["Empty String Padding ('') for Missing Atoms"]
    Universe["Universal Atom Types (37 total)"] --> Types["atom_types (src/common/residue_constants.py:1-6)"]
    Types --> Order["atom_order (src/common/residue_constants.py:7)"]
```
*Sources: [src/common/residue_constants.py:1-38]()*

---

## 3. Chemical and Hydrogen Bonding Constants

Physical and chemical parameters used for surface analysis, atomic radii assignment, and hydrogen bond geometry are defined in `atom_constants.py` (adapted from MaSIF) [src/common/atom_constants.py:1-151]().

* **Atomic Radii (`radii`)**: Dictionary mapping element symbols (`'N'`, `'O'`, `'C'`, `'H'`, `'S'`, `'P'`), pseudo-atoms (`'Z'`), and disembodied points (`'X'`) to floating-point radius values [src/common/atom_constants.py:7-17]().
* **Polar Hydrogens (`polarHydrogens`)**: Maps 3-letter residue codes to lists of polar hydrogen atom names recognized by reduction programs (e.g., SER maps to `['H', 'HG']`, PRO maps to `[]`) [src/common/atom_constants.py:19-39]().
* **Hydrogen Bond Geometry**: 
  * `hbond_std_dev`: Standard deviation for angular distributions ($\pi / 3$) [src/common/atom_constants.py:41]().
  * `acceptorAngleAtom`: Maps acceptor atoms to their directly bonded reference atoms for angle calculations [src/common/atom_constants.py:45-51]().
  * `acceptorPlaneAtom`: Maps acceptor atoms to third reference atoms for plane determination [src/common/atom_constants.py:53-54]().
  * `donorAtom`: Maps hydrogen/donor atoms to their parent donor groups (e.g., `'HH11'` maps to `'NH1'`) [src/common/atom_constants.py:56-151]().

*Sources: [src/common/atom_constants.py:1-151]()*

---

# Page: Tensor and DDP Utilities

# Tensor and DDP Utilities

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/model/components/triangle_update.py](src/model/components/triangle_update.py)
- [src/model/optimizer.py](src/model/optimizer.py)
- [src/utils/ddp_utils.py](src/utils/ddp_utils.py)
- [src/utils/model_utils.py](src/utils/model_utils.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope
This page details the shared utility functions and classes located in `src/utils/model_utils.py` and `src/utils/ddp_utils.py`. These modules provide core tensor manipulation primitives, recursive tensor tree mapping utilities for complex nested data structures, distributed multi-process state management wrappers, and global reproducibility seeding routines.

---

## Model Tensor Utilities (`src/utils/model_utils.py`)

The `src/utils/model_utils.py` module defines tensor reshaping, expansion, padding, dimension movement functions, and recursive tree mapping operations used throughout the model architecture.

### Shape Manipulation Helpers

- **`expand_at_dim(x, dim, n)`**: Expands a tensor `x` along a specified `dim` by repeating it `n` times using `unsqueeze` and `expand` [src/utils/model_utils.py:8-25]().
- **`pad_at_dim(x, dim, pad_length, value)`**: Pads a tensor along dimension `dim` with left and right padding amounts defined by `pad_length` [src/utils/model_utils.py:27-54]().
- **`reshape_at_dim(x, dim, target_shape)`**: Reshapes a specific dimension `dim` of a tensor into `target_shape` while preserving all surrounding dimensions [src/utils/model_utils.py:57-79]().
- **`move_final_dim_to_dim(x, dim)`**: Permutes a tensor to relocate its final dimension to an arbitrary target dimension `dim` [src/utils/model_utils.py:81-106]().

Sources: `src/utils/model_utils.py`

### Recursive Tensor Tree Mapping

To facilitate operations on arbitrarily nested structures (such as dictionaries, lists, and tuples containing PyTorch tensors), `src/utils/model_utils.py` provides recursive tree traversal functions:

- **`dict_map(fn, dic, leaf_type)`**: Recursively traverses a dictionary, applying `tree_map` to non-dictionary leaf nodes and recursing into sub-dictionaries [src/utils/model_utils.py:108-116]().
- **`tree_map(fn, tree, leaf_type)`**: Inspects the type of `tree`. If it is a `dict`, `list`, or `tuple`, it recurses over its elements; if it matches `leaf_type`, it applies `fn(tree)` [src/utils/model_utils.py:119-130]().
- **`tensor_tree_map`**: A pre-configured `partial` application of `tree_map` where `leaf_type` is fixed to `torch.Tensor` [src/utils/model_utils.py:132-132]().

```mermaid
graph TD
    Root["Input Tree (dict/list/tuple)"] --> Check{"Is instance of leaf_type?"}
    Check -- "No (Container)" --> Recurse["Traverse dict / list / tuple"]
    Recurse --> Root
    Check -- "Yes (torch.Tensor)" --> Apply["Apply fn(Tensor)"]
    Apply --> Output["Return Transformed Tree"]
```
*Figure 1: Recursive execution flow of `tree_map` and `tensor_tree_map` over nested data structures.*

Sources: `src/utils/model_utils.py`

---

## Distributed Data Processing Utilities (`src/utils/ddp_utils.py`)

The `src/utils/ddp_utils.py` module handles distributed environment initialization checks, process rank resolution, object gathering across distributed nodes, and deterministic random seeding.

### Distributed State and `DistWrapper`

- **`distributed_available()`**: Returns `True` if `torch.distributed` is both available and initialized [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:8-10]().
- **`DistWrapper`**: A class that inspects environment variables (`RANK`, `LOCAL_RANK`, `LOCAL_WORLD_SIZE`, `WORLD_SIZE`) to compute process topology parameters including global rank, local rank, world size, number of nodes, and node rank [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:12-20]().
- **`DIST_WRAPPER`**: A module-level singleton instance of `DistWrapper` [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:34-34]().
- **`DistWrapper.all_gather_object(obj, group)`**: Gathers arbitrary Python objects across all processes in the world using `torch.distributed.all_gather_object` when distributed training is active, or returns a single-item list containing `obj` otherwise [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:21-32]().

Sources: `src/utils/ddp_utils.py`

### Reproducibility and Seeding

- **`seed_everything(seed, deterministic)`**: Seeds `random`, `numpy`, `torch`, and `torch.cuda`. When `deterministic=True`, it disables `cudnn.benchmark`, sets `cudnn.deterministic = True`, enforces `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`, and configures `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG` to ensure reproducible execution on CUDA devices [src/utils/ddp_utils.py:37-49]().

```mermaid
graph TD
    Env["Environment Variables (RANK / WORLD_SIZE)"] --> DW["DistWrapper.__init__()"]
    DW --> Singleton["DIST_WRAPPER Instance"]
    Singleton --> Gather["DistWrapper.all_gather_object()"]
    
    Seed["seed_everything(seed, deterministic)"] --> PyRNG["random, numpy, torch seeds"]
    Seed --> Det{"deterministic == True?"}
    Det -- "Yes" --> CUDNN["cudnn.deterministic = True & use_deterministic_algorithms()"]
```
*Figure 2: Distributed environment configuration via `DistWrapper` and global reproducibility control via `seed_everything`.*

Sources: `src/utils/ddp_utils.py`

---

# Page: Glossary

# Glossary

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [scripts/prepare_afdb_entries.py](scripts/prepare_afdb_entries.py)
- [scripts/prepare_inference_embeddings.py](scripts/prepare_inference_embeddings.py)
- [scripts/uniprot_sprot.fasta.gz](scripts/uniprot_sprot.fasta.gz)
- [src/data/dataset.py](src/data/dataset.py)
- [src/model/loss.py](src/model/loss.py)
- [src/model/surpass.py](src/model/surpass.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page provides formal definitions of domain-specific concepts, structural biology terminology, and codebase jargon used across the `SurPass` repository. Each entry links directly to the underlying classes, functions, and configuration parameters in the source code.

---

## 1. Architectural and Modeling Jargon

### Distogram
A **distogram** is a two-dimensional matrix of probability distributions over discrete pairwise distance bins for all residue pairs in a protein complex [src/model/loss.py:113-128](). In `SurPass`, the distogram output logits are generated by projecting the pair representation tensor through a linear layer and layer normalization [src/model/surpass.py:120-121]() and are supervised via cross-entropy [src/model/loss.py:123-128]() or focal loss [src/model/loss.py:131-171]().

### Contact Bins
**Contact bins** define the contiguous subset of distance bins at the lower end of the distogram (e.g., distances $< 8.0\,\text{Å}$) that denote physical inter-residue contacts [src/model/loss.py:84-92](). The integer parameter `contact_bins` specifies the cutoff index separating contacting pairs from non-contacting pairs [src/model/surpass.py:44-45]().

### Intra / Inter Mask
* **`intra_mask`**: A Boolean tensor indicating residue pairs belonging to the same protein chain [src/model/loss.py:151]().
* **`inter_mask`**: A Boolean tensor indicating residue pairs spanning two different interacting chains [src/model/loss.py:152]().
These masks decouple intra-chain folding supervision from inter-chain protein-protein interaction (PPI) supervision during multi-objective loss computation [src/model/loss.py:171]().

### QKLN (Query-Key Layer Normalization)
**QKLN** refers to Query-Key Layer Normalization applied directly to query and key projections within multi-head attention mechanisms (`use_qkln=True`) [src/model/surpass.py:38,84]() to stabilize training dynamics and prevent attention logit explosion in deep transformer stacks.

### $r_{\max}$ (Maximum Relative Position Encoding)
$r_{\max}$ defines the maximum clipping distance or relative sequence separation window used by the `ResidueEmbedder` when constructing relative positional encodings between residues [src/model/components/embedder.py]().

### Outer Product Mean (OPM)
The **Outer Product Mean** (`EfficientOuterProductMean`) is a module that bridges the single residue stream ($\mathbf{m}$) and the pair stream ($\mathbf{z}$) by computing outer products of single representations across channel dimensions, updating pair features at each layer [src/model/surpass.py:90-96]() [src/model/components/outer_product_mean.py]().

### Triangle Updates (Incoming / Outgoing)
**Triangle updates** (`TriangleMultiplicationOutgoing` and `TriangleMultiplicationIncoming`) update the pair representation $\mathbf{z}$ using triangular relational reasoning along incoming and outgoing edges of the residue pair graph [src/model/surpass.py:98-110]() [src/model/components/triangle_update.py]().

### EMA (Exponential Moving Average)
**EMA** maintains a shadow copy of model parameters updated as an exponential moving average of training weights, stabilizing evaluation and inference checkpoints [4.3]().

---

## 2. Biological and Data Pipeline Jargon

### PPI Cluster
A **PPI cluster** is a group of protein-protein interaction pairs clustered by sequence and interface similarity (via MMSeqs2) to prevent data leakage between training, validation, and test splits [src/data/dataset.py:30,62-76](). The dataset loads samples indexed by `ppi_cluster_id` [src/data/dataset.py:63,72]().

### AFDB (AlphaFold Database)
**AFDB** refers to local collections of AlphaFold Database domain structures utilized to extract experimental and predicted structural features for training complexes [scripts/prepare_afdb_entries.py:2-13]().

### pLM / ESMC (Protein Language Model)
**pLM / ESMC** refers to Evolutionary Scale Modeling protein language model embeddings (`plm_emb`) extracted from amino acid sequences, providing rich evolutionary and biochemical context as inputs to the `ResidueEmbedder` [scripts/prepare_inference_embeddings.py:1-4]() [src/model/components/embedder.py]().

### Atom14 Representation
**Atom14** is a fixed 14-atom coordinate and mask schema per residue used internally for structural feature extraction and geometric validation [scripts/prepare_afdb_entries.py:44-46]().

### CB Positions ($C_\beta$)
**$C_\beta$ positions** (`cb_positions`, `cb_mask`) denote the 3D coordinates and validity masks of carbon-beta atoms (or carbon-alpha for Glycine) utilized for inter-residue distance calculations and ground-truth label generation [scripts/prepare_afdb_entries.py:50-51]().

### Tversky Loss
**Tversky loss** is an asymmetric generalization of the Dice coefficient used to handle severe class imbalance between positive contact pairs and negative non-contact pairs [src/model/loss.py]().

### Noisy-OR
**Noisy-OR** is a probabilistic aggregation function used to combine multi-residue or windowed predictions into global protein-level interaction scores.

### Long-Sequence Windowing
**Windowing** (`plan_ppi_windows`) is a spatial tiling strategy that divides exceptionally long protein complexes into manageable sub-windows to fit within GPU memory constraints during inference [5.2]().

---
